summary: Assigns algorithm identifiers to the HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF), specified in RFC 5869, when used with three common hash functions. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: HKDF turns one secret into many keys. This gives names to its versions so programs can say which one they use.

questions: what are the hkdf object identifiers
subtitle: Gives HKDF, a key derivation function, three official names so protocols can say which hash it uses.

tldr.problem: HKDF is specified in RFC 5869, but some security protocols such as the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) need an algorithm identifier to name the algorithm they use, and HKDF had none.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns three object identifiers, one for HKDF used with each of SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, and defines an ASN.1 module that declares them.
tldr.outcome: Protocols that carry an AlgorithmIdentifier can now name HKDF with one of these three hashes. The parameters component is always absent.

today: RFC 8619 is a Proposed Standard from June 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of these HKDF algorithm identifiers.

sections.title: Why HKDF Needs Identifiers
sections.content:
The HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF) is specified in RFC 5869. It is a key derivation function built on the Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC).

RFC 8619 does not change HKDF. It only assigns algorithm identifiers to HKDF when it is used with three common one-way hash functions. The RFC says these identifiers are needed to make use of HKDF in some security protocols, such as the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) defined in RFC 5652.

Values in the document are generated with ASN.1 using the Basic Encoding Rules (BER) and the Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER).
sections.eli5: A recipe book already describes how HKDF works. This document just writes a label on each version so other programs can point at the one they mean.

sections.title: The Three Algorithm Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC assigns three object identifiers, one for HKDF used with each hash function from the Secure Hash Standard: SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512. All three sit under the same S/MIME algorithms arc (smime(16) alg(3)) and differ only in the last number: 28, 29 and 30.

When any of these identifiers appears in the ASN.1 type AlgorithmIdentifier, the parameters component of that type SHALL be absent. In other words, the identifier alone says everything: which key derivation function and which hash.

The definition of AlgorithmIdentifier is available in RFC 5911, which evolved from the original definition in X.509.
sections.eli5: There are three name tags, one for each size of hash. The tag already says everything, so nothing else needs to be attached to it.

sections.title: The ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
Section 3 holds an ASN.1 module named HKDF-OID-2019. It imports AlgorithmIdentifier{} and KEY-DERIVATION from the AlgorithmInformation-2009 module, which is defined in RFC 5912.

The module repeats the three object identifiers, then defines kda-hkdf-with-sha256, kda-hkdf-with-sha384 and kda-hkdf-with-sha512 as KEY-DERIVATION objects. Each one gives its identifier, states PARAMS ARE absent and lists S/MIME capabilities identified by the same OID. A set called KeyDevAlgs collects the three and is marked extensible.
sections.eli5: This is the official form that lists the three name tags in a way computers can read, and says none of them carries extra notes.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is brief here. It notes that, despite the simplicity of HKDF, many security considerations were taken into account in its design and analysis, and that an exposition of all of them is well beyond the scope of the document.

Readers who want the details, including the rationale for the HKDF design, are pointed to Krawczyk's paper "Cryptographic Extraction and Key Derivation: The HKDF Scheme" (CRYPTO 2010).
sections.eli5: The authors say the safety reasoning is long and lives somewhere else, and they tell you which paper to read.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
One object identifier for the ASN.1 module was assigned in the "SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifiers (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.0)" registry: id-mod-hkdf-oid-2019, number 68.

The three algorithm identifiers (28, 29 and 30) were assigned in the "SMI Security for S/MIME Algorithms (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.3)" registry.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper wrote down the module and the three name tags so nobody else can use the same numbers.
